explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - OmniParse is primarily a backend-focused, monolithic Python service that ingests arbitrary unstructured data (documents, images, audio/video, web pages) and converts it into structured, GenAI-ready outputs via deep-learning models.  
   - It also provides a Python client SDK, a CLI for model download and server startup, and an ("interactive") Gradio UI.  

2. Analyze the file structure  
   - Top-level artifacts:  
     • server.py         – main FastAPI (or similar) HTTP server entrypoint  
     • download.py       – CLI to preload models  
     • Dockerfile        – containerization  
     • omniparse/        – core modules by domain (chunking, documents, extraction, image, media, web, models, utils)  
     • python-sdk/       – client library that wraps HTTP calls to the server  
     • docs/             – user/developer documentation & examples  
     • examples/         – Colab notebook for end-to-end demo  
   - The omniparse package follows a “router + handler + model” pattern: each subfolder (e.g., `omniparse/documents/router.py`, `omniparse/image/router.py`, `omniparse/media/router.py`, `omniparse/web/router.py`) registers endpoints, delegates to domain-specific processing modules, which in turn invoke preloaded DL models.  

3. Examine README for additional insights  
   - CLI flags `--documents`, `--media`, `--web` control which modules (and therefore which heavy models) are loaded into GPU memory at startup.  
   - Exposed REST endpoints under `/parse_document`, `/parse_media`, `/parse_image`, `/parse_website` correspond one-to-one to the routers.  
   - No persistent database is used – data flows in (file or URL), is processed in memory via models, and results are returned immediately.  

4. Main components and interactions  
   a. Clients:  
      - Python SDK (`python-sdk/`)  
      - REST/HTTP clients (curl, Postman)  
      - CLI (`download.py`, `server.py` flags)  
      - Gradio UI (embedded or launched by server)  
   b. API Server Layer (`server.py` + FastAPI/Starlette):  
      - API Gateway accepts HTTP requests → dispatches to domain routers  
   c. Domain Routers & Handlers:  
      - Document Router  
      - Image Router  
      - Media Router  
      - Web Router  
      - (Optional) Sheets Router  
   d. Processing Modules:  
      - Chunking (`omniparse/chunking/`)  
      - Extraction (`omniparse/extraction/`)  
      - OCR & Layout (Surya OCR series, Florence-2)  
      - Whisper for audio/video transcription  
      - Web crawler (Selenium-based)  
   e. Model Manager & GPU Resource:  
      - Central loader orchestrates model fetch (via `download.py`) and maintains them in GPU memory (with caching)  
   f. File System & External Services:  
      - Local disk for temporary file storage  
      - Selenium / headless browser for web crawling  
   g. Output Layer:  
      - Structured Markdown / JSON returned over HTTP  
      - (Optionally) streamed back to Gradio UI or Python SDK  

5. Architectural patterns & design principles  
   - Modular router pattern: clearly separated REST endpoints match to domain routers, simplifying adding new data-type support.  
   - Plugin-style model loading: CLI flags selectively load heavy models, reducing startup footprint.  
   - Separation of concerns: API layer vs. processing layer vs. model management.  
   - Stateless request handling: no database–the service is horizontally scalable (multiple container instances behind a load balancer).  

6. Tailoring the diagram to OmniParse  
   - Emphasize the single Backend service box (monolith) with sub-modules inside it.  
   - Show the Python SDK as an external client calling HTTP.  
   - Illustrate the optional Gradio UI on the same server or as a separate front-end block calling the API.  
   - Highlight the Model Manager as a separate component inside the server, with arrows to ML frameworks (Torch, Whisper, Surya OCR).  
   - Include the Docker container boundary around the server + models.  

7. Elements to include in your diagram  
   - Clear labels: “API Gateway (FastAPI)”, “Document Router”, “Image Router”, “Model Manager”, “GPU Memory”, “Python SDK (client)”, “CLI”  
   - Directional arrows:  
       • Client → API Gateway → Domain Router → Processing Module → Model Manager → GPU  
       • Model Manager → Processing Module → Router → Response → Client  
   - Color coding:  
       • Blue rectangles for server internals (modules, routers)  
       • Green cylinder for model storage / GPU resources  
       • Orange for external clients (SDK, CLI, UI)  
       • Grey for external services (Selenium, local FS)  

8. Step-by-step diagram creation guidelines  
   1. Draw the container boundary (“Docker Container” or “K8s Pod”) around the server.  
   2. Inside, at the top, place “API Gateway (server.py / FastAPI)”.  
   3. Below it, array the four Domain Routers in parallel: Documents, Images, Media, Web.  
   4. Beneath each router, draw its dependent Processing Modules (chunking, extraction, OCR, transcription, crawling).  
   5. To the side, draw “Model Manager & GPU Memory” (cylinder + GPU icon) with arrows pointing to each Processing Module.  
   6. Outside the container, place:  
      - Python SDK (HTTP client)  
      - CLI tools (`download.py`, `server.py` launcher)  
      - Gradio UI (if used externally)  
      - Selenium WebDriver (for Web Router)  
   7. Connect them with directional arrows showing request/response flow.  
   8. Apply color-coding and shapes per component type.  
   9. Add annotations for dynamic model loading flags (`--documents`, `--media`, `--web`).  

With this layout, a reader immediately grasps:  
   - How clients interact via HTTP  
   - How requests route to specialized modules  
   - How the heavy ML models are managed centrally  
   - That it’s a stateless, horizontally scalable monolith inside Docker  

This level of detail ensures your system-diagram captures all essential architectural elements without overcomplicating the view.
</explanation>
